title: Money and its Role
summary: The barter system is the exchange of one kind of goods and services for another, with no money involved. It is a sign of ancient civilisation. Examples: European traders exchanged fur and crafts for eastern perfumes and silk; tribal families in India exchange labour for labour at harvest; farmers, artisans, cobblers and carpenters swapped their products.
## Demerits of barter: the need for money
(1) Lack of double coincidence of wants. A person with rice who wants cloth must find someone who has cloth and also wants rice. Such a person is rarely found, and searching for one wastes time.
(2) Lack of divisibility. A cow cannot be cut up to buy small amounts of cloth or grain.
(3) No common measure of value. Because there is no common unit, it is hard to equate the values of different goods — how many yards of cloth is a cow worth?
(4) Storage. A farmer had to store large amounts of wheat in a warehouse to trade day by day.
(5) No store of value. Goods such as salt and vegetables perish and lose value, so they could not be used for future payments or lending.
These problems led people to adopt money, a common medium that is easy to carry, store and use to express value.
Money is anything generally accepted by society as a medium of exchange, which also acts as a unit of account, a store of value and a means of repaying debt. It has four functions.
(1) Medium of exchange, the primary function: goods are bought and sold for money. You pay ₹10 for a pen, so the pen is exchanged for ₹10. This removes the need for double coincidence of wants.
(2) Measure of value (unit of account): the value of a good is expressed in money. Value = price × quantity: a 25 kg bag of rice at ₹20 a kg is worth ₹500.
(3) Store of value: money holds purchasing power for later. Sushila cannot store mangoes, but she can store the ₹250 she got by selling them.

(4) Standard of deferred payments: loans are repaid in money at a future date, with interest. A friend borrows ₹300 and repays ₹301 after a week. A used book would not be accepted in repayment, but money keeps its value.

Over time, money has taken the form of cattle, salt, and gold, silver and copper coins. Today it is paper currency notes, coins and bank deposits (cheques). Indian notes are rupees, with the symbol ₹. Smaller amounts are paise (50 paise is half a rupee), and coins go up to ₹10.

Currency notes and coins are guaranteed by the Government of India. One-rupee notes and coins are issued by the Ministry of Finance; all other notes are issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Indian currency is valid only in India.
Other currencies: USA — dollar ($); Europe — euro (€); United Kingdom — pound (£); Japan — yen (¥); China — yuan.

sa: Explain money as a standard of deferred payment with an example.

Money is used to make payments in the future. A friend borrows ₹300 to buy a book and promises to repay it after a week with ₹1 interest, i.e. ₹301.
The lender accepts money because it keeps its value; a used book would not be accepted.
So loans and future payments are settled in money.
What is money? State two of its functions.

Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange, which also serves as a unit of account, a store of value and a means of repaying debt.
(1) Medium of exchange: goods are bought and sold for money.
(2) Measure of value: prices and values of goods are expressed in money.
'The lack of double coincidence of wants is a common problem with the barter system.' Explain.

In barter, the person with rice who wants cloth must find someone who has cloth and wants rice.
Such a match is rare, so exchange often does not take place and much time is wasted searching, especially when transport and communication were poor.
Money solves this, since anyone accepts money for their goods.
Explain the main demerits of the barter system.

(1) Lack of double coincidence of wants.
(2) Lack of divisibility — a cow cannot be split.
(3) No common measure of value.
(4) Large stocks had to be stored for trade.
(5) Perishable goods could not store value, so lending and future payment were not possible.
la: Explain the functions of money: medium of exchange and measure of value.

Medium of exchange: the primary function. People sell goods for money and use money to buy other goods; you pay ₹10 for a pen and the seller receives ₹10. Exchange no longer needs a double coincidence of wants, and buying and selling become quick and easy.
Measure of value: money is the common unit of account. The value of every good is expressed in money, value = price × quantity — a 25 kg bag of rice at ₹20 a kg is worth ₹500. This makes comparison, accounting and pricing simple, which was not possible under barter.
Why did the need for money arise? Explain the demerits of barter.

Money arose because barter failed.
(1) Lack of double coincidence of wants — a matching trader was hard to find.
(2) Lack of divisibility — a cow cannot be divided to buy small items.
(3) No common measure of value — values of different goods could not be equated.
(4) Storage — large stocks of goods had to be kept in warehouses.
(5) No store of value — perishable goods lost value, so lending and future payment were impossible.
People therefore adopted money, a common medium that is easy to carry and store and that expresses value.
